entries.69b9841d657524aa1d798b3351dbf3ff95fce46b: <div sID="gen19915" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Hos.12" sID="Hos.12"/> <div eID="gen19915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19916" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19917" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A high charge drawn up against both Israel and Judah for their sins, which were the ground of God's controversy with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1-Hos.12.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. Particularly the sin of fraud and injustice, which Ephraim is charged with (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">ver. 7</reference>), and justifies himself in, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">ver. 8</reference>. And the sin of idolatry (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">ver. 11</reference>), by which God is provoked to contend with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.14">ver. 14</reference>. II. The aggravations of the sins they are charged with, taken from the honour God put upon their father Jacob (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.3-Hos.12.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), the advancement of them into a people from low and mean beginnings (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.12-Hos.12.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>), and the provision he had made them of helps for their souls by the prophets he sent them, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.10">ver. 10</reference>. III. A call to the unconverted to turn to God, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.6">ver. 6</reference>. IV. An intimation of mercy that God had in store for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">ver. 9</reference>.
entries.068c56175b94ae106085e77308788cd32701b156: <div eID="gen19917" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19916" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Crimes of Israel and Judah; Expostulations with Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 723.)</title> <div sID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Ephraim feedeth on wind, and followeth after the east wind: he daily increaseth lies and desolation; and they do make a covenant with the Assyrians, and oil is carried into Egypt. <hi type="super">2</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath also a controversy with Judah, and will punish Jacob according to his ways; according to his doings will he recompense him. <hi type="super">3</hi> He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God: <hi type="super">4</hi> Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him <hi type="italic">in</hi> Bethel, and there he spake with us; <hi type="super">5</hi> Even the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of hosts; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> his memorial. <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore turn thou to thy God: keep mercy and judgment, and wait on thy God continually. <div eID="gen19918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen19919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19920" type="x-p"/> I. Ephraim is convicted of folly, in staying himself upon Egypt and Assyria, when he was in straits (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Ephraim feeds on wind,</hi> that is, feeds himself with vain hopes of assistance from man, when he is at variance with God; and, when he meets with disappointments, he still pursues the same game, and greedily pants and <hi type="italic">follows after the east wind,</hi> which he cannot catch holy of, nor, if he could, would it be nourishing, nay, would be noxious. We say of the <hi type="italic">wind in the east,</hi> It is <hi type="italic">good neither for man nor beast.</hi> It was said (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">ch. viii. 7</reference>), He <hi type="italic">sows the wind;</hi> and as he sows so he reaps (He <hi type="italic">reaps the whirlwind</hi>); and as he reaps so he feeds—He feeds on the wind, the <hi type="italic">east wind.</hi> Note, Those that make creatures their confidence make fools of themselves, and take a great deal of pains to put a cheat upon their own souls and to prepare vexation for themselves: <hi type="italic">He daily increaseth lies,</hi> that is, multiplies his correspondences and leagues with his neighbours, which will all prove deceitful to him; nay, they will prove desolation to him. Those very nations that he makes his refuge will prove his ruin. Those that stay themselves upon lies will be still coveting to increase them, that they may build their hopes firmly upon them; as if many lies twisted together would make one truth, or many broken reeds and rotten supports one sound one, which is a great delusion and will prove to them a great desolation; for those that <hi type="italic">observe lying vanities</hi> the more they increase them the more disappointments they prepare for themselves and the further they run from <hi type="italic">their own mercies.</hi> The men of Ephraim did so when they thought to secure the Assyrians in their interests by a <hi type="italic">solemn league,</hi> signed, sealed, and sworn to: <hi type="italic">They make a covenant with the Assyrians,</hi> but they will find there is no hold of them; that potent prince will be a slave to his word no longer than he pleases. They thought to secure the Egyptians for their confederates by a rich present of the commodities of their country, not only to purchase their favour, but to show that their friendship was worth having: <hi type="italic">Oil is carried into Egypt.</hi> But the Egyptians, when they had got the bribe, dropped the cause, and Ephraim was never the better for them. <hi type="italic">Oleum perdidit et operam—The oil and the labour are both lost.</hi> This was <hi type="italic">feeding on wind;</hi> this was <hi type="italic">increasing lies and desolation.</hi> <div eID="gen19920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19921" type="x-p"/> II. Judah is contended with too, and Jacob, which includes both Ephraim and Judah (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord has also a controversy with Judah;</hi> for though he had a while ago <hi type="italic">ruled with God,</hi> and been <hi type="italic">faithful with the saints,</hi> yet now he begins to degenerate. Or though, in keeping close to the house of David and the house of Aaron, and in them to the covenants of royalty and priesthood, they were so far <hi type="italic">in the right,</hi> in the former they <hi type="italic">ruled with God</hi> and in the latter were <hi type="italic">faithful to the saints,</hi> yet upon other accounts God <hi type="italic">had a controversy</hi> with them, and would punish them. Note, Men's being in the right in some things, in the main things, will not exempt them from correction, and therefore should not exempt them from reproof, for those things wherein they are in the wrong. There were those of the seven churches of Asia whom Christ approved and commended, and yet he adds, <hi type="italic">Nevertheless I have something against thee.</hi> So here; though the seed of Jacob are a people near to God, yet God will punish them according to the evil ways they are found in and the evil doings they are found guilty of; for God sees sin even in his own people, and will reckon with them for it. <div eID="gen19921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19922" type="x-p"/> III. Both Ephraim and Judah are put in mind of their father Jacob, whose seed they were and whose name they bore (and it was their honour), of the extraordinary things which he did and which God did for him, that they might be the more ashamed of themselves for degenerating from so illustrious a progenitor and staining the lustre of so great a name, and yet that they might be engaged and encouraged to return to God, the God of their father Jacob, in hopes for his sake to find favour with him. He had called this people Jacob (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">v. 2</reference>), threatening to punish them; but <hi type="italic">how shall I give them up?</hi> How shall that dear name be forgotten? <div eID="gen19922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19923" type="x-p"/> 1. Three glorious things concerning Jacob the person Jacob the people are here put in mind of; but by brief hints only, for it is presumed that they knew the story:—(1.) His struggling with Esau in the womb: There <hi type="italic">he took his brother by the heel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.12.3">v. 3</reference>. We have the story <reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">Gen. xxv. 26</reference>. It was an early act of bravery, and an effort for the best precedency, a pious ambition for that birthright in the covenant which Esau is justly branded as profane for despising. But his degenerate seed, by mingling with the nations, and making leagues with them, profaned that crown, and laid that honour in the dust, which he so gloriously put in for. Then it was that the dominion was given to him: <hi type="italic">The elder shall serve the younger.</hi> Then he was owned of God as his beloved: <hi type="italic">Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.</hi> But they had by their sin forfeited both the love of God and dominion over their neighbours. (2.) His wrestling with the angel. "Remember how your father Jacob had <hi type="italic">power with God by his</hi> own <hi type="italic">strength,</hi> the strength he had by the gift of God, who <hi type="italic">pleaded</hi> not <hi type="italic">against him by his great power,</hi> but <hi type="italic">put strength into him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.22.6">Job xxii. 6</reference>. The angel he wrestled with is called <hi type="italic">God,</hi> and therefore is supposed to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God,</hi> the angel of the covenant. "God was both a combatant with Jacob and an assistant of him, showing, in the latter respect, greater strength than in the former, fighting as it were against him with his left hand and for him with his right, and to that putting greater force." So, Dr. Pocock. The providence of God fought against him when he met with one danger after another, in his return homewards; but the grace of God enabled him to go on cheerfully in his way, and, when his faith acted upon the divine promise that was for him prevailed above his fears that arose from the divine providences that wee against him, then <hi type="italic">by his strength he had power with God.</hi> But it refers especially to his prayer for deliverance from Esau, and for a blessing: <hi type="italic">He had power over the angel and prevailed,</hi> for he <hi type="italic">wept and made supplication.</hi> Here was a mixture of the greatest courage and the greatest tenderness, Jacob wrestling like a champion and yet weeping like a child. Note, Prayers and tears are the weapons with which the saints have obtained the most glorious victories. Thus Jacob commenced <hi type="italic">Israel—a prince with God;</hi> his posterity was called <hi type="italic">Israel,</hi> but they were unworthy the name, for they had forfeited and lost their communion with God, and their interest in him, by revolting from their duty to him. (3.) His meeting with God at Bethel: God <hi type="italic">found him</hi> in Bethel, <hi type="italic">and there he spoke with us.</hi> God found him the first time in Bethel, as he went to Padanaram (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.10">Gen. xxviii. 10</reference>), and a second time after his return, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.9">Gen. xxxv. 9</reference>, &c. It is probable that this refers to both; for in both God spoke to Jacob, and renewed the covenant with him, and the prophet might very well say, <hi type="italic">There he spoke with us</hi> who are the seed of Jacob, for both times that God spoke with Jacob at Bethel he spoke with him concerning his seed. <reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">Gen. xxviii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Gen.35.12">Gen. xxxv. 12</reference>, <hi type="italic">This land I will give unto thy seed.</hi> Thus God then covenanted with him and his seed after him. Now justly are they upbraided with this; for in that very place which their father Jacob called <hi type="italic">Bethel—the house of God,</hi> in remembrance of the communion he there had with God, did they set up one of the calves, and worship it; thus they turned that Bethel into a <hi type="italic">Beth-aven</hi>—a <hi type="italic">house of iniquity.</hi> There God <hi type="italic">spoke with them</hi> exceedingly great and precious promises, which they had despised and lost the benefit of. <div eID="gen19923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> 2. Two inferences are here drawn from these stories concerning Jacob, for instruction to his seed:— <div eID="gen19924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is a use of information. From what passed between God and Jacob we may learn that <hi type="italic">Jehovah, the Lord God of hosts,</hi> is <hi type="italic">the God of Israel;</hi> he was the God of Jacob, and this is <hi type="italic">his memorial</hi> throughout all the generations of the seed of Jacob (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.5">v. 5</reference>)—the more shame for those who forgot the memorial of their church, deserted the God of their fathers, and exchanged a <hi type="italic">Lord of hosts</hi> for Baalim. Note, Those only are accounted the people of God that keep up a memorial of God, such a memorial of him as he himself has instituted, by which he makes himself known and will have us to remember him. Here are two memorials of his, by which he is distinguished from all others, and is to be acknowledged and adored by us. [1.] The former denotes his <hi type="italic">existence of himself.</hi> He is Jehovah, much the same with <hi type="italic">I AM,</hi> the same that <hi type="italic">was, and is, and is to come,</hi> infinite, eternal, and unchangeable. Jehovah is <hi type="italic">his memorial,</hi> his peculiar name. [2.] The latter denotes his dominion over all: He is the <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> that has all the hosts of heaven and earth at his beck and command, and makes what use he pleases of them. Jacob saw <hi type="italic">Mahanaim</hi>—God's <hi type="italic">two hosts,</hi> about the time that he <hi type="italic">wrestled with the angel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.1-Gen.32.2">Gen. xxxii. 1, 2</reference>), and so learned to call God the <hi type="italic">God of hosts,</hi> and transmitted it to us as his memorial. God's names, titles, and attributes, are the memorials of him; there is no need for images to be such. And that which was a revelation of God to one is his memorial to many, to all generations. <div eID="gen19925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19926" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is a use of exhortation, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.6">v. 6</reference>. "Is this so, that Jacob thy father had this communion with the Lord God of hosts, and is this still his memorial?" Then, [1.] Let those that have gone astray from God be converted to him: <hi type="italic">Therefore turn thou to thy God.</hi> He that was the God of Jacob is the God of Israel, is <hi type="italic">thy God;</hi> from him thou hast unjustly and unkindly revolted; therefore turn thou to him by repentance and faith, turn to him as thine, to love him, obey him, and depend upon him. [2.] Let those that are converted to him walk with him in all holy conversation and godliness: "<hi type="italic">Keep mercy and judgment,</hi> mercy in relieving and succouring the poor and distressed, judgment in rendering to all their due; be kind to all; do wrong to none. <hi type="italic">Keep piety and judgment</hi>" (so it may be read); "live <hi type="italic">righteously and godly in this present world;</hi> be devout and be honest. Do not only practise these occasionally, but be careful, and constant, and conscientious in the practice of them." [3.] Let those that walk with God be encouraged to live a life of dependence upon him: "<hi type="italic">Wait on thy God continually,</hi> with a believing expectation to receive from him all the succours and supplies thou standest in need of." Those that live a life of conformity to God may live a life of confidence and comfort in him, if it be not their own fault. Let our <hi type="italic">eyes</hi> be <hi type="italic">ever towards the Lord,</hi> and let us preserve a holy security and serenity of mind under the protection of the divine power and the influence of the divine favour, looking, without anxiety, for a dubious event, and by faith keeping our spirits sedate and even; this is waiting on God as our God in covenant, and this we must do continually.
entries.a91fe4373699dffbb0840374f107b08646179cdd: <div eID="gen19926" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Reproof for Sin; Judgment Threatened; Memorials of Divine Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 723.)</title> <div sID="gen19927" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="italic">He is</hi> a merchant, the balances of deceit <hi type="italic">are</hi> in his hand: he loveth to oppress. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out substance: <hi type="italic">in</hi> all my labours they shall find none iniquity in me that <hi type="italic">were</hi> sin. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I <hi type="italic">that am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God from the land of Egypt will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles, as in the days of the solemn feast. <hi type="super">10</hi> I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets. <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> iniquity <hi type="italic">in</hi> Gilead? surely they are vanity: they sacrifice bullocks in Gilgal; yea, their altars <hi type="italic">are</hi> as heaps in the furrows of the fields. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept <hi type="italic">sheep.</hi> <hi type="super">13</hi> And by a prophet the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet was he preserved. <hi type="super">14</hi> Ephraim provoked <hi type="italic">him</hi> to anger most bitterly: therefore shall he leave his blood upon him, and his reproach shall his Lord return unto him. <div eID="gen19927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> Here are intermixed, in these verses, <div eID="gen19928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> I. Reproofs for sin. When God is coming forth to contend with a people, that he may demonstrate his own righteousness, he will demonstrate their unrighteousness. Ephraim was called to turn to his God and <hi type="italic">keep judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.6">v. 6</reference>); now, to show that he had need of that call, he is charged with turning from his God by idolatry, and breaking the laws of justice and judgment. <div eID="gen19929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> 1. He is here charged with injustice against the precepts of the second table, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7-Hos.12.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen19930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> (1.) What the sin is wherewith he is charged: <hi type="italic">He is a merchant.</hi> The margin reads it as a proper name, <hi type="italic">He is Canaan,</hi> or a Canaanite, unworthy to be denominated from Jacob and Israel, and worthy to be cast out with a curse from this good land, as the Canaanites were. See <reference osisRef="Amos.9.7">Amos ix. 7</reference>. But Canaan sometimes signifies <hi type="italic">a merchant,</hi> and therefore is most likely to do so here, where Ephraim is charged with deceit in trade. Though God had given his people a land flowing with milk and honey, yet he did not forbid them to enrich themselves by merchandise, and they succeeded the Canaanites in that as well as in their husbandry; they sucked <hi type="italic">the abundance of the seas and the treasures hidden in the sand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.19">Deut. xxxiii. 19</reference>. And, if they had been fair merchants, it would have been no reproach at all to them, but an honour and a blessing. But he is such a merchant as the Canaanites were, who were honest only with good looking to, and, if they could, cheated all they dealt with. Ephraim does so; he deceives and thereby oppresses. Note, There is oppression by fraud as well as oppression by force. It is not only princes, lords, and masters, that oppress their subjects, tenants, and servants, but merchants and traders are often guilty of oppressing those they deal with, when they impose upon their ignorance, or take advantage of their necessity, to make hard bargains with them, or are rigorous and severe in exacting their debts. Ephraim cheated, [1.] With a great deal of art and cunning: <hi type="italic">The balances of deceit are in his hand.</hi> He uses balances, and delivers his goods by weight and measure, as if he would be very exact, but they are balances of deceit, false weights and false measures, and thus, under colour of doing right, he does the greatest wrong. Note, God has his eye upon merchants and traders, when they are weighing their goods and paying their money, whether they do honestly or deceitfully. He observes what balances they have in their hand, and how they hold them; and, though those they deal with may not be aware of that sleight of hand with which they make them balances of deceit, God sees it, and knows it. Trades by the wit of man are made <hi type="italic">mysteries,</hi> but it is a pity that by the sin of man they should ever be made <hi type="italic">mysteries of iniquity.</hi> [2.] With a great deal of pleasure and pride: <hi type="italic">He loves to oppress.</hi> To oppress is bad enough, but to love to do so is much worse. His conscience does not check and reprove him for it, as it ought to do; if it did, though he committed the sin, he could not delight in it; but his corruptions are so strong, and have so triumphed over his convictions, that he not only loves the gain of oppression, but he loves to oppress, sins for sinning-sake, and takes a pleasure in out-witting and over-reaching those that suspect him not. <div eID="gen19931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19932" type="x-p"/> (2.) How he justifies himself in this sin, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">v. 8</reference>. Wicked men will have something to say for themselves now when they are told of their faults, some frivolous turn-off or other wherewith to evade the convictions of the word. Ephraim stands indicted for a common cheat. Now see what he pleads to the indictment. He does not deny the charge, nor plead, Not guilty, yet does not make a penitent confession of it and ask pardon, but insists upon his own justification. Suppose it were so that he did use balances of deceit, yet, [1.] He pleads that he had got a good estate. Let the prophet say what he pleased of his deceit, of the sin of it and the curse of God that attended it, he could not be convinced there was any harm or danger in it, for this he was sure of that he had thriven in it: "<hi type="italic">Yet I have become rich, I have found me out substance.</hi> Whatever you make of it, I have made a good hand of it." Note, Carnal hearts are often confirmed in a good opinion of their evil ways by their worldly prosperity and success in those ways. But it is a great mistake. Every word in what Ephraim says here proclaims his folly. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is folly to call the riches of this world substance, for they are things that are not, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is folly to think that we have them of ourselves, to say (as some read it), <hi type="italic">I have made myself rich;</hi> what <hi type="italic">substance</hi> I have is owing purely to my ingenuity and industry—<hi type="italic">I have found it; my might and the power of my hand have gotten me this wealth. Thirdly,</hi> It is folly to think that what we have is for ourselves. <hi type="italic">I have found me out substance,</hi> as if we had it for our own proper use and behoof, whereas we hold it in trust, only as stewards. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> It is folly to think that riches are things to be gloried in, and to say with exultation, <hi type="italic">I have become rich.</hi> Riches are not the honours of the soul, are not peculiar to the best men, nor sure to us; and therefore <hi type="italic">let not the rich man glory in his riches,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.1.9-Jas.1.10">Jam. i. 9, 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> It is folly to think that growing rich in a sinful way makes us innocent, or will make us safe, or may make us easy, in that way; for the prosperity of fools deceives and destroys them. See <reference osisRef="Isa.47.10">Isa. xlvii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.32">Prov. i. 32</reference>. [2.] He pleads that he had kept a good reputation. It is common for sinners, when they are justly reproved by their ministers, to appeal to their neighbours, and because they know no ill of them, or will say none, or think well of what the prophets charge them with as bad, fly in the face of their reprovers: <hi type="italic">In all my labours</hi> (says Ephraim) <hi type="italic">they shall find no iniquity in me that were sin.</hi> Note, Carnal hearts are apt to build a good opinion of themselves upon the fair character they have among their neighbours. Ephraim was very secure; for, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> All his neighbours knew him to be diligent in his business; they had an eye upon <hi type="italic">all his labours,</hi> and commended him for them. <hi type="italic">Men will praise thee when thou doest well for thyself. Secondly,</hi> None of them knew him to be deceitful in his business. He acted with so much policy that nobody could say to the contrary but that he acted with integrity. For either, 1. He concealed the fraud, so that none discovered it: "Whatever iniquity there is, <hi type="italic">they shall find</hi> none;" as if no iniquity were displeasing to God, and damning to the soul, but that which is open and scandalous before men. What will it avail us that men shall find no iniquity in us, when God finds a great deal, and will bring every secret work, even secret frauds, into judgment? Or, 2. He excused the fraud, so that none condemned it: "<hi type="italic">They shall find no iniquity in me that were sin,</hi> nothing very bad, nothing but what is very excusable, only some venial sins, sins not worth speaking of," which they think God will make nothing of because they do not. It is a fashionable iniquity; it is customary; it is what every body does; it is pleasant; it is gainful; and this, they think, is no iniquity that is sin; nobody will think the worse of them for it. But God sees not as man sees; he judges not as man judges. <div eID="gen19932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19933" type="x-p"/> 2. He is here charged with idolatry, against the precepts of the first table, with that iniquity which is in a special manner vanity, the making and worshipping of images, which are vanities (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Surely they are vanity;</hi> they do not profit, but deceive. Now the prophet mentions two places notorious for idolatry:—(1.) Gilead on the other side Jordan, which had been branded for it before (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">ch. vi. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Is there iniquity in Gilead?</hi> It is a thing to be wondered at; it is a thing to be sadly lamented. What! iniquity in Gilead? idolatry there? Gilead was a fruitful pleasant country (pleasant to a proverb, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.6">Jer. xxii. 6</reference>), and does it so ill requite the Lord? It was a frontier-country, and lay much exposed to the insults of enemies, and therefore stood in special need of the divine protection; what! and yet by iniquity throw itself out of that protection? <hi type="italic">Is there iniquity in Gilead?</hi> Yea, (2.) And in Gilgal too; there they <hi type="italic">sacrifice bullocks</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.5">ch. ix. 15</reference>), and there <hi type="italic">their altars</hi> which they have set up, either to strange gods in opposition to his own appointed altar, are as thick <hi type="italic">as heaps</hi> of manure <hi type="italic">in the furrows of the field</hi> that is to be sown, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Is there iniquity in Gilead</hi> only? so some. Is it only in those remote parts of the nation that people are so superstitious, where they border upon other nations? No; they are as bad at Gilgal. In Gilead God protected Jacob their father (of whom he had been speaking) from the rage of Laban; and will you there commit iniquity? <div eID="gen19933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19934" type="x-p"/> II. Here are threatenings of wrath for sin. Some make that to be so (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will make thee to dwell in tabernacles as in the days of the appointed time,</hi> that is, I will bring thee into such a condition as the Israelites were in when they dwelt in tents and wandered for forty years; that was the <hi type="italic">time appointed</hi> in <hi type="italic">the wilderness.</hi> Ephraim forgot that God brought him out of Egypt and brought him up to be what he was, and was proud of his wealth, and took sinful courses to increase it; and therefore God threatens to bring him to a tabernacle-state again, to a poor, mean, desolate, unsettled condition. Note, It is just with God, when men have by their sins turned their tents into houses, by his judgments to turn their houses into tents again. However, that is certainly a threatening (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly.</hi> See how men are deceived in their opinion of themselves, and how they will one day be undeceived. Ephraim thought that there was no iniquity in him that deserved to be called sin (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">v. 8</reference>); but God told him that there was that in him which was sin, and would be found so if he did not repent and reform; for, 1. It was extremely offensive to his God: <hi type="italic">Ephraim provoked him to anger most bitterly</hi> with his iniquities, which were so distasteful to God, and to him too would be <hi type="italic">bitterness in the latter end.</hi> He was so wilful in sinning against his knowledge and convictions that any one might see, and say, that he designed no other than to provoke God in the highest degree. 2. It would certainly be destructive to himself; that cannot be otherwise which provokes God against him, and kindles the fire of his wrath. Therefore, (1.) He shall take away his forfeited life: <hi type="italic">He shall leave his blood upon him,</hi> that is, he shall not hold him guiltless, but bring upon him that death which is the wages of sin. <hi type="italic">His blood shall be upon his own head</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.16">2 Sam. i. 16</reference>), for his own iniquity has testified against him and he alone shall bear it. Note, When sinners perish their blood is left upon them. (2.) He shall take away his forfeited honour: <hi type="italic">His reproach shall his Lord return upon him.</hi> God is <hi type="italic">his Lord;</hi> he had by idolatry and other sins reproached the Lord, and done dishonour to him, and to his name and family, and had given occasion to others to reproach him; and now God will return the reproach upon him, according to the word he has spoken, that <hi type="italic">those who despise him shall be lightly esteemed.</hi> Note, Shameful sins shall have shameful punishments. If Ephraim put contempt on his God, he shall be so reduced that all his neighbours shall look with contempt upon him. <div eID="gen19934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19935" type="x-p"/> III. Here are memorials of former mercy, which come in to convict them of base ingratitude in revolting from God. Let them blush to remember, <div eID="gen19935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19936" type="x-p"/> 1. That God had raised them from meanness. When Ephraim had become rich, and was proud of that, he forgot that which God (that he might not forget it) obliged them every year to acknowledge (<reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">Deut. xxvi. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">A Syrian ready to perish was my father.</hi> But God here puts them in mind of it, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.12">v. 12</reference>. Let them remember, not only the honours of their father Jacob, what a <hi type="italic">mighty prince</hi> he was with God, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.3">v. 3</reference> (an honour which they had no share in while they were in rebellion against God), but what a poor servant he was to Laban, which was sufficient to mortify those that were puffed up with the estates they had raised. <hi type="italic">Jacob fled into Syria</hi> from a malicious brother, and there served a covetous uncle <hi type="italic">for a wife,</hi> and <hi type="italic">for a wife he kept sheep,</hi> because he had not estate to endow a wife with. Jacob was poor, and low, and a fugitive; therefore his posterity ought not to be proud. He was a plain man, dwelling in tents, and keeping sheep; therefore <hi type="italic">balances of deceit</hi> ill became them. He <hi type="italic">served for a wife</hi> that was not a Canaanitess, as Esau's wives were; therefore it was a shame for them to degenerate into Canaanites, and mingle with the nations. God wonderfully preserved him in his flight and preserved him in his service, so that he multiplied exceedingly, and from that <hi type="italic">root</hi> in a dry ground sprang an illustrious nation, that bore his name, which magnifies the goodness of God both to him and them and leaves them under the stain of base ingratitude to that God who was their founder and benefactor. <div eID="gen19936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> 2. That God had rescued them from misery, had raised them to what they were, not only out of poverty, but out of slavery (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.13">v. 13</reference>), which laid them under much stronger obligations to serve him and under a yet deeper guilt in serving other gods. (1.) God <hi type="italic">brought Israel out of Egypt</hi> on purpose that they might serve him, and by redeeming them out of bondage acquired a special title to them and to their service. (2.) He preserved them, as sheep are kept by the shepherd's care. He preserved them from Pharaoh's rage at the sea, even at the Red Sea, protected them from all the perils of the wilderness, and provided for them. (3.) He did this <hi type="italic">by a prophet,</hi> Moses, who, though he is called <hi type="italic">king in Jeshurun</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deut. xxxiii. 5</reference>), yet did what he did for Israel <hi type="italic">as a prophet,</hi> by direction from God and by the power of his word. The ensign of his authority was not a royal sceptre, but the <hi type="italic">rod of God;</hi> with that he summoned both Egypt's plagues and Israel's blessings. Moses, as a prophet, was a type of Christ (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.22">Acts iii. 22</reference>), and it is by Christ as a prophet that we are brought out of the Egypt of sin and Satan by the power of his truth. Now this shows how very unworthy and ungrateful this people were, [1.] In rejecting their God, who had brought them out of Egypt, which, in the preface to the commandments, is particularly mentioned as a reason for the first, why they should have no other gods before him. [2.] In despising and persecuting his prophets, whom they should have loved and valued, and have studied to answer God's end in sending them, for the sake of that prophet by whom God had brought them out of Egypt and preserved them in the wilderness. Note, The benefit we have had by the word of God greatly aggravates our sin and folly if we put any slight upon the word of God. <div eID="gen19937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> 3. That God had taken care of their education as they grew up. This instance of God's goodness we have, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.10">v. 10</reference>. As by a prophet he delivered them, so <hi type="italic">by prophets</hi> he still continued to speak to them. Man, who is formed out of the earth, is fed out of the earth; so that nation, that was formed by prophecy, by prophecy was fed and taught; <hi type="italic">beginning at Moses,</hi> and so going on <hi type="italic">to all the prophets</hi> through the several ages of that church, we find that divine revelation was all along their tuition. (1.) They had prophets raised up among themselves (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">Amos ii. 11</reference>), a succession of them, were scarcely ever without a Spirit of prophecy among them more or less, from Moses to Malachi. (2.) These prophets were <hi type="italic">seers;</hi> they had <hi type="italic">visions,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dreams,</hi> in which God discovered his mind to them immediately, with a full assurance that it was his mind, <reference osisRef="Num.12.6">Num. xii. 6</reference>. (3.) These visions were multiplied; God spoke not only <hi type="italic">once, yea, twice,</hi> but many a time; if one vision was not regarded, he sent another. The prophets had variety of visions, and frequent repetitions of the same. (4.) God <hi type="italic">spoke</hi> to them <hi type="italic">by the prophets.</hi> What the prophets <hi type="italic">received from the Lord</hi> they plainly and faithfully delivered to them. The people at Mount Sinai begged that God would speak to them by men like themselves, and he did so. (5.) In speaking to them by the prophets he <hi type="italic">used similitudes,</hi> to make the messages he sent by them intelligible, more affecting, and more likely to be remembered. The visions they saw were often similitudes, and their discourses were embellished with very apt comparisons. And, as God by his prophets, so by his Son, he <hi type="italic">used similitudes,</hi> for <hi type="italic">he opened his mouth in parables.</hi> Note, God keeps an account, whether we do or no, of the sermons we hear; and those that have long enjoyed the means of grace in purity, plenty, and power, that have been frequently, faithfully, and familiarly, told the mind of God, will have a great deal to answer for another day if they persist in a course of iniquity. <div eID="gen19938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19939" type="x-p"/> IV. Here are intimations of further mercy, and this remembered too in the midst of sin and wrath (as some understand <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I that am the Lord thy God from the land of Egypt,</hi> who then and there took thee to be my people, and have approved myself thy God ever since, in a constant series of merciful providences, have yet a kindness for thee, bad as thou art; and I will <hi type="italic">make thee to dwell in tabernacles,</hi> not as in the wilderness, but <hi type="italic">as in the days of the solemn feast,</hi>" the feast of tabernacles, which was celebrated with great joy, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.40">Lev. xxiii. 40</reference>. 1. They shall be made to see, by the grace of God, that though they are rich, and have found out substance, yet they are but in a tabernacle-state, and have in their worldly wealth <hi type="italic">no continuing city.</hi> 2. They shall yet have cause to rejoice in God, and have opportunity to do it in public ordinances. The feast of tabernacles was the first solemn feast the Jews kept after their return out of Babylon, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.4">Ezra iii. 4</reference>. 3. This, as other promises, was to have its full accomplishment in the grace of the gospel, which provides tabernacles for believers in their way to heaven, and furnishes them with matter of joy, holy joy, joy in God, such as was in the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18-Zech.14.19">Zech. xiv. 18, 19</reference>.  <chapter eID="Hos.12"/> <div eID="gen19939" type="x-p"/>

entries.c36a4dddd87c86d1aec966389d45066440f62ef2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12396"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.12.1-Hos.12.14">Ho 12:1-14</reference>. Reproof of Ephraim and Judah: Their Father Jacob Ought to Be a Pattern to Them.</title> <div sID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> This prophecy was delivered about the time of Israel's seeking the aid of the Egyptian king So, in violation of their covenant with Assyria (see <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>). He exhorts them to follow their father Jacob's persevering prayerfulness, which brought God's favor upon him. As God is unchangeable, He will show the same favor to Jacob's posterity as He did to Jacob, if, like him, they seek God.<div eID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22714" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12396"/><hi type="bold">1. feedeth on wind--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Prov.15.14">Pr 15:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">Is 44:20</reference>). Followeth after vain objects, such as alliances with idolaters and their idols (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.8.7">Ho 8:7</reference>).<div eID="gen22714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">east wind--</hi>the simoon, blowing from the desert east of Palestine, which not only does not benefit, but does injury. Israel follows not only things vain, but things pernicious (compare <reference osisRef="Job.15.2">Job 15:2</reference>).<div eID="gen22715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">increaseth lies--</hi>accumulates lie upon lie, that is, impostures wherewith they deceive themselves, forsaking the truth of God.<div eID="gen22716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desolation--</hi>violent oppressions practised by Israel [Maurer]. Acts which would prove the cause of Israel's own desolation [Calvin].<div eID="gen22717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covenant with ... Assyrians--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">Ho 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">7:11</reference>).<div eID="gen22718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oil ... into Egypt--</hi>as a present from Israel to secure Egypt's alliance (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Is 30:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.9">57:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>). Palestine was famed for oil (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>). <div eID="gen22719" type="x-p"/>
entries.52a595fe08307cbddaf47bf6e80639f35fa8dc9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12397"/><div sID="gen22720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12397"/><hi type="bold">2. controversy with Judah--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.4.1">Ho 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.2">Mi 6:2</reference>). Judah, under Ahaz, had fallen into idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.3">2Ki 16:3</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen22720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jacob--</hi>that is, the ten tribes. If Judah, the favored portion of the nation, shall not be spared, much less degenerate Israel. <div eID="gen22721" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca985c5a1755d1f993c93139bb294dff2956c983: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12398"/><div sID="gen22722" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12398"/><hi type="bold">3. He--</hi>Jacob, contrasted with his degenerate descendants, called by his name, Jacob (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Ho 12:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>). He took Esau by the heel in the womb in order to obtain, if possible, the privileges of the first-born (<reference osisRef="Gen.25.22-Gen.25.26">Ge 25:22-26</reference>), whence he took his name, Jacob, meaning "supplanter"; and again, by his strength, prevailed in wrestling with God for a blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.24-Gen.32.29">Ge 32:24-29</reference>); whereas ye disregard My promises, putting your confidence in idols and foreign alliances. He conquered God, ye are the slaves of idols. Only have Jehovah on your side, and ye are stronger than Edom, or even Assyria. So the spiritual Israel lays hold of the heel of Jesus, "the First-born of many brethren," being born again of the Holy Spirit. Having no right in themselves to the inheritance, they lay hold of the bruised heel, the humanity of Christ crucified, and let not go their hold of Him who is not, as Esau, a curse (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.16">He 12:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.17">17</reference>), but, by becoming a curse for us, is a blessing to us.<div eID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">power with God--</hi>referring to his name, "Israel," prince of God, acquired on that occasion (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.12">Mt 11:12</reference>). As the promised Canaan had to be gained forcibly by Israel, so heaven by the faithful (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.13.24">Lu 13:24</reference>). "Strive," literally, "as in the agony of a contest." So the Canaanitess (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>).<div eID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his strength--</hi>which lay in his conscious weakness, whence, when his thigh was put out of joint by God, he hung upon Him. To seek strength was his object; to grant it, God's. Yet God's mode of procedure was strange. In human form He tries as it were to throw Jacob down. When simple wrestling was not enough, He does what seems to ensure Jacob's fall, dislocating his thigh joint, so that he could no longer stand. Yet it was then that Jacob prevailed. Thus God teaches us the irresistible might of conscious weakness. For when weak in ourselves, we are strong by His strength put in us (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.5">Is 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">2Co 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen22724" type="x-p"/>
entries.9168ac68251b188fb2d03bb8e9c096ad158bd962: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12399"/><div sID="gen22725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12399"/><hi type="bold">4. the angel--</hi>the uncreated Angel of the Covenant, as God the Son appears in the Old Testament (Mal 3:1).<div eID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made supplication--</hi><reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Ge 32:26</reference>: "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me."<div eID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22727" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he found him--</hi>The angel found Jacob, when he was fleeing from Esau into Syria: the Lord appearing to him "in Beth-el" (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.11-Gen.19.35">Ge 28:11-19; 35</reference>:1). What a sad contrast, that in this same Beth-el now Israel worships the golden calves!<div eID="gen22727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there he spake with us--</hi>"with us," as being in the loins of our progenitor Jacob (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">Psa 66:6</reference>, "They ... we;" <reference osisRef="Heb.7.9">He 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.10">10</reference>). What God there spoke to Jacob appertains to us. God's promises to him belong to all his posterity who follow in the steps of his prayerful faith. <div eID="gen22728" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac516543946e05c78bfc0320b58a3f47f64d5b00: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12400"/><div sID="gen22729" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12400"/><hi type="bold">5. Lord God--</hi>Jehovah, a name implying His immutable constancy to His promises. From the Hebrew root, meaning "existence." "He that is, was, and is to be," always the same (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">He 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.4">Re 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.8">8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.3.14">Ex 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">6:3</reference>). As He was unchangeable in His favor to Jacob, so will He be to His believing posterity.<div eID="gen22729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of hosts--</hi>which Israel foolishly worshipped. Jehovah has all the hosts (saba) or powers of heaven and earth at His command, so that He is as all-powerful, as He is faithful, to fulfil His promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">Psa 135:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.27">Am 5:27</reference>).<div eID="gen22730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22731" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">memorial--</hi>the name expressive of the character in which God was ever to be remembered (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.13">Psa 135:13</reference>). <div eID="gen22731" type="x-p"/>
entries.22b34df22fd005c0a129d1b6b071e198b4f68df6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12401"/><div sID="gen22732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12401"/><hi type="bold">6. thou--</hi>who dost wish to be a true descendant of Jacob.<div eID="gen22732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to THY God--</hi>who is therefore bound by covenant to hear thy prayers.<div eID="gen22733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep mercy and judgment--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Mic.6.8">Mi 6:8</reference>). These two include the second-table commandments, duty towards one's neighbor, the most visible test of the sincerity on one's repentance.<div eID="gen22734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wait on thy God--</hi>alone, not on thy idols. Including all the duties of the first table (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.3">Psa 37:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">5, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.1">40:1</reference>). <div eID="gen22735" type="x-p"/>
entries.a0be12faa3ccb5c865a5da636896a9708cb7f417: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12402"/><div sID="gen22736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12402"/><hi type="bold">7. merchant--</hi>a play on the double sense of the Hebrew, "Canaan," that is, a Canaanite and a "merchant" <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.3">Eze 16:3</reference>: "Thy birth is ... of Canaan." They who naturally were descendants of pious Jacob had become virtually Canaanites, who were proverbial as cheating merchants (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.11">Is 23:11</reference>, Margin), the greatest reproach to Israel, who despised Canaan. The Phoenicians called themselves Canaanites or merchants (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Is 23:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oppress--</hi>open violence: as the "balances of deceit" imply fraud. <div eID="gen22737" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a17599cbe762223b06035500803169cd96782e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12403"/><div sID="gen22738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12403"/><hi type="bold">8. And--</hi>that is, Notwithstanding.<div eID="gen22738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Yet I am ... rich--</hi>I regard not what the prophets say: I am content with my state, as I am rich (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.17">Re 3:17</reference>). Therefore, in just retribution, this is the very language of the enemy in being the instrument of Israel's punishment. <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">Zec 11:5</reference>: "They that sell them say ... I am rich." Far better is poverty with honesty, than riches gained by sin.<div eID="gen22739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my labours--</hi>my gains by labor.<div eID="gen22740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22741" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they shall find none--</hi>that is, none shall find any.<div eID="gen22741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity ... that were sin--</hi>iniquity that would bring down the penalty of sin. Ephraim argues, My success in my labors proves that I am not a guilty sinner as the prophets assert. Thus sinners pervert God's long-suffering goodness (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>) into a justification of their impenitence (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.11-Eccl.8.13">Ec 8:11-13</reference>). <div eID="gen22742" type="x-p"/>
entries.71c752aa528e1435010f8f5f6c4bc61a398c4984: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12404"/><div sID="gen22743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12404"/><hi type="bold">9. And--</hi>rather, "And yet." Though Israel deserves to be cast off for ever, yet I am still what I have been from the time of My delivering them out of Egypt, their covenant God; therefore, "I will yet make thee to dwell in tabernacles," that is, to keep the feast of tabernacles again in remembrance of a new deliverance out of bondage. Fulfilled primarily at the return from Babylon (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.17">Ne 8:17</reference>). Fully and antitypically to be fulfilled at the final restoration from the present dispersion (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.16">Zec 14:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Lev.23.42">Le 23:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.43">43</reference>). <div eID="gen22743" type="x-p"/>
entries.23c605228110fb8bf9cdebaddef4178991c1e120: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12405"/><div sID="gen22744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12405"/><hi type="bold">10. by ... the prophets--</hi>literally, "upon," that is, My spirit resting on them. I deposited with them My instructions which ought to have brought you to the right way. An aggravation of your guilt, that it was not through ignorance you erred, but in defiance of God and His prophets [Calvin]. Ahijah the Shilonite, Shemaiah, Iddo, Azariah, Hanani, Jehu, Elijah, Elisha, Micaiah, Joel, and Amos were "the prophets" before Hosea.<div eID="gen22744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visions ... similitudes--</hi>I adopted such modes of communication, adapted to man's capacities, as were calculated to arouse attention: I left no means untried to reform you. The first, second, and third chapters contain examples of "similitudes." <div eID="gen22745" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fb962bdcc09e91784d3c131e744ab02b3f554f0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12406"/><div sID="gen22746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12406"/><hi type="bold">11. Is there iniquity in Gilead?--</hi>He asks the question, not as if the answer was doubtful, but to strengthen the affirmation: "Surely they are vanity"; or as Maurer translates, "They are nothing but iniquity." Iniquity, especially idolatry, in Scripture is often termed "vanity." <reference osisRef="Prov.13.11">Pr 13:11</reference>: "Wealth gotten by vanity," that is, iniquity. <reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">Is 41:29</reference>: "They are all vanity ... images." "Gilead" refers to Mizpah-gilead, a city representing the region beyond Jordan (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.8">Ho 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.11.29">Jud 11:29</reference>); as "Gilgal," the region on this side of Jordan (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.15">Ho 4:15</reference>). In all quarters alike they are utterly vile.<div eID="gen22746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their altars are as heaps in the furrows--</hi>that is, as numerous as such heaps: namely, the heaps of stones cleared out of a stony field. An appropriate image, as at a distance they look like altars (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Ho 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.11">8:11</reference>). As the third member in the parallelism answers to the first, "Gilgal" to "Gilead," so the fourth to the second, "altars" to "vanity." The word "heaps" alludes to the name "Gilgal," meaning "a heap of stones." The very scene of the general circumcision of the people, and of the solemn passover kept after crossing Jordan, is now the stronghold of Israel's idolatry. <div eID="gen22747" type="x-p"/>
entries.4216b09b2b9e871075da6a1377e7cff97b1fcf12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12407"/><div sID="gen22748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12407"/><hi type="bold">12. Jacob fled ... served--</hi>Though ye pride yourselves on the great name of "Israel," forget not that your progenitor was the same Jacob who was a fugitive, and who served for Rachel fourteen years. He forgot not ME who delivered him when fleeing from Esau, and when oppressed by Laban (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.5">Ge 28:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.29.20">29:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.26.5">De 26:5</reference>). Ye, though delivered from Egypt (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.13">Ho 12:13</reference>), and loaded with My favors, are yet unwilling to return to Me.<div eID="gen22748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">country of Syria--</hi>the champaign region of Syria, the portion lying between the Tigris and Euphrates, hence called Mesopotamia. Padan-aram means the same, that is, "Low Syria," as opposed to Aramea (meaning the "high country") or Syria (<reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Ge 48:7</reference>). <div eID="gen22749" type="x-p"/>
entries.c11014ef0aa455cbc6113ea4da6241da0db35555: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12408"/><div sID="gen22750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12408"/><hi type="bold">13. by a prophet--</hi>Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.12.6-Num.12.8">Nu 12:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.18.15">De 18:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen22750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preserved--</hi>Translate, "kept"; there is an allusion to the same Hebrew word in <reference osisRef="Hos.12.12">Ho 12:12</reference>, "kept sheep"; Israel was kept by God as His flock, even as Jacob kept sheep (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.1">Psa 80:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Is 63:11</reference>). <div eID="gen22751" type="x-p"/>
entries.434ef50d53d3b6de6f33c69ea41f79055662a48b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12409"/><div sID="gen22752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12409"/><hi type="bold">14. provoked him--</hi>that is, God.<div eID="gen22752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leave his blood upon him--</hi>not take away the guilt and penalty of the innocent blood shed by Ephraim in general, and to Molech in particular.<div eID="gen22753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his reproach shall his Lord return unto him--</hi>Ephraim's dishonor to God in worshipping idols, God will repay to him. That God is "his Lord" by right redemption and special revelation to Ephraim only aggravates his guilt, instead of giving him hope of escape. God does not give up His claim to them as His, however they set aside His dominion. <chapter eID="Hos.12"/>

entries.a8ab4e554b52022ba996007964f4aaf2bef691f3: <div eID="gen33889" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33890" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33891" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33891" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33890" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33892" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in very pointed terms, describes the unprofitableness and destruction attending vicious courses; particularly such as Ephraim pursued, who forsook God, and courted the alliance of idolatrous princes, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos 12:1</reference>. Judah is also reproved, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Hos 12:2</reference>. He is reminded of the extraordinary favor of God to his father Jacob, in giving him the birthright; and exhorted, after his example, to wrestle with God (the Angel of the covenant, the same unchangeable Jehovah) for a blessing; and to love mercy and execute justice, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.3-Hos.12.4">Hos 12:3-4</reference>. Ephraim is accused of pursuing practices that are deceitful, although pretending to integrity, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.7">Hos 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Hos 12:8</reference>. God then threatens to deprive this people of their possessions, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">Hos 12:9</reference>, as they had rejected every means of reformation, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.10">Hos 12:10</reference>, and given themselves up to gross impieties, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Hos 12:11</reference>. And, as an aggravation of their guilt, they are reminded from what humble beginnings they had been raised, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.12">Hos 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.13">Hos 12:13</reference>. The Divine judgments about to fall upon Israel are declared to be the result of great provocation, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.14">Hos 12:14</reference>. <div eID="gen33892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33893" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33894" type="x-p"/> Ephraim feedeth on wind - He forms and follows empty and unstable counsels. <div eID="gen33894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33895" type="x-p"/> Followeth after the east wind - They are not only empty, but dangerous and destructive. The east wind was, and still is, in all countries, a parching, wasting, injurious wind. <div eID="gen33895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33896" type="x-p"/> He daily increaseth lies - He promises himself safety from foreign alliances. He "made a covenant with the Assyrians," and sent a subsidy of "oil to Egypt." The latter abandoned him; the former oppressed him.
entries.61f6b1d9748c168e58dca02e03e0202b8afedaf1: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33897" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath also a controversy with Judah - The rest of the prophecy belongs both to Judah and Israel. He reproaches both with their ingratitude, and threatens them with God's anger. In order to make their infidelity the more hateful, and their malice the more sensible, he opposes to them the righteousness, obedience, and piety of their father Jacob. He recalls to their minds the benefits they had received since they returned from Egypt. He speaks afterwards of their kings; and how, in their ingratitude, they refused to have him for their monarch. Having mentioned this fact, he subjoins reflections, exhortations, invectives, and threatenings, and continues this subject in this and the two following chapters. - Calmet.
entries.2a27da0616887d8073edc2940c57eaba54c2e83c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33898" type="x-p"/> He took his brother by the heel - See on <reference osisRef="Gen.25.26">Gen 25:26</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen 32:24</reference> (note), etc.
entries.0c9bbe3a820ba3d1ca9fe8e5aa098607c3e0aa24: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33899" type="x-p"/> He had power over the Angel - Who represented the invisible Jehovah. <div eID="gen33899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33900" type="x-p"/> He wept, and made supplication - He entreated with tears that God would bless him; and he prevailed. The circumstance of his weeping is not mentioned in Genesis. <div eID="gen33900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33901" type="x-p"/> He found him in Beth-el - It was there that God made those glorious promises to Jacob relative to his posterity. See <reference osisRef="Gen.28.13-Gen.28.15">Gen 28:13-15</reference>.
entries.9babdad6f876013393d5deee0cbd61cf9de6fae2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33902" type="x-p"/> The Lord is his memorial - He is the same God as when Jacob so successfully wrestled with him.
entries.5e2ac4e725a45e4a6077a00597301460f5006d0f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33903" type="x-p"/> Therefore turn thou to thy God - Because he is the same, and cannot change. Seek him as faithfully and as fervently as Jacob did, and you will find him the same merciful and compassionate Being.
entries.ac661609d1302853dc2121bbc5805af10e80c877: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33904" type="x-p"/> He is a merchant - Or a Canaanite; referring to the Phoenicians, famous for their traffic. Ephraim is as corrupt as those heathenish traffickers were. He kept, as many in all ages have done, a weight and a weight; a heavy one to buy with and a light one to sell by.
entries.27d23f0640da0451907f390e77dec347d9596471: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33905" type="x-p"/> I am become rich - They boasted in their riches, notwithstanding the unjust manner in which they were acquired. <div eID="gen33905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33906" type="x-p"/> In all my labors they shall find none iniquity in me - This is frequently the language of merchants, tradesmen, etc. None are so full of professions of equity and justice, while all the time they are endeavoring to overreach, both in buying and selling. "Sir, I cannot afford it at that price." "It is not mine for that money." "I assure you that it cost me more than you offer." "I am sorry I cannot take your money; but if I did, I should lose by the article," etc., etc., etc. I have heard such language over and over, when I knew every word was false. Truth is a sacred thing in the sight of God; but who regards it as he should? There are, however, many noble exceptions among merchants and tradesmen. Bp. Newcome gives another turn to the subject, by translating: - "All his labors shall not be found profitable unto him, <div eID="gen33906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33907" type="x-p"/> For the iniquity wherewith he hath sinned."
entries.4026ea8c6483c2d50ecd47397b46283ccf66f642: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33908" type="x-p"/> And I - the Lord thy God - I who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, will again make thee to dwell in tabernacles. This appears to be a threatening. I will reduce you to as miserable a state in the land of your captivity, as you often were through your transgressions in the wilderness. This was the opinion of some of the ancients on this verse; and the context requires it to be understood in this way. I do not think that the feast of tabernacles is referred to.
entries.6c51ac263d23e102281bf94287935072bfa1206a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33909" type="x-p"/> I have also spoken - I have used every means, and employed every method, to instruct and save you. I have sent prophets, who spake plainly, exhorting, warning, and beseeching you to return to me. They have had Divine visions, which they have declared and interpreted. They have used similitudes, symbols, metaphors, allegories, etc., in order to fix your attention, and bring you back to your duty and interest. And, alas! all is in vain; you have not profited by my condescension. This text St. Paul seems to have had full in view, when he wrote, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">Heb 1:1</reference> (note): "God who, at Sundry Times and in Divers Manners, spake in time past unto the Fathers by the Prophets." See the note on the above. <div eID="gen33909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33910" type="x-p"/> Dr. Dodd supposes that there are three distinct kinds of prophecy mentioned here: <div eID="gen33910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33911" type="x-p"/> 1. Immediate inspiration, when God declares the very words. <div eID="gen33911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33912" type="x-p"/> 2. Vision; a representation of external objects to the mind, in as lively a manner as if there were conveyed by the senses. <div eID="gen33912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33913" type="x-p"/> 3. Parables and apt resemblances.
entries.7a9e7e6fad455a9ac452654d931d2a0e1f15250d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33914" type="x-p"/> Iniquity in Gilead - Gilgal and Gilead are equally iniquitous, and equally idolatrous. Gilead, which was beyond Jordan, had already been brought under subjection by Tiglath-Pileser. Gilgal, which was on this side Jordan, shall share the same fate; because it is now as idolatrous as the other. <div eID="gen33914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33915" type="x-p"/> Their altars are as heaps - They occur everywhere. The whole land is given to idolatry.
entries.13c59373f409f845f20dff772e7de06738f96327: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33916" type="x-p"/> Served for a wife - Seven years for Rachel. <div eID="gen33916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33917" type="x-p"/> For a wife he kept sheep - Seven years for Leah; having been cheated by Laban, who gave him first Leah, instead of Rachel; and afterwards made him serve seven years more before he would confirm his first engagement. Critics complain of want of connection here. Why is this isolated fact predicted? Thus, in a detached sentence, the prophet speaks of the low estate of their ancestors, and how amply the providence of God had preserved and provided for them. This is all the connection the place requires.
entries.a235c62977c6897a174b998d5e8e77ad6e51ebb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen33917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33918" type="x-p"/> By a prophet (Moses) the Lord brought Israel out of Egypt, and by a prophet (Joshua) was he preserved - Joshua succeeded Moses, and brought the Israelites into the promised land; and when they passed the Jordan at Gilgal, he received the covenant of circumcision; and yet this same place was now made by them the seat of idolatry! How blind and how ungrateful!
entries.750ad4952405f711099a37a564f82f2c90a1ae45: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen33918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33919" type="x-p"/> Therefore shall he leave his blood upon him - He will not remove his guilt. These are similar to our Lord's words, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.36">Joh 3:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.9.41">Joh 9:41</reference> : "He that believeth not on the Son of God, shall not see life, for the wrath of God Abideth On Him" - shall not be removed by any remission, as he rejects the only way in which he can be saved. Because ye say, We see; therefore, Your Sin Remaineth, i.e., it still stands charged against you. Your miseries and destruction are of your own procuring; your perdition is of yourselves. God is as merciful as he is just.  <chapter eID="Hos.12"/> <div eID="gen33919" type="x-p"/>

entries.540ae089cf0ff1b390c6c578610aade8d7509ab4: <div eID="gen16259" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">3. Israel’s Apostasy and God’s Fidelity - Hosea 12-14</title> <div sID="gen16260" type="x-p"/> For the purpose of proving that the predicted destruction of the kingdom is just and inevitable, the prophet now shows, in this last division, first that Israel has not kept the ways of its father Jacob, but has fallen into the ungodly practice of Canaan (Hos 12:1-14); and secondly, that in spite of all the manifestations of love, and all the chastisements received from its God, it has continued its apostasy and idolatry, and therefore perfectly deserves the threatened judgment. Nevertheless the compassion of God will not permit it to be utterly destroyed, but will redeem it even from death and hell (ch. 13-14:1). To this there is appended, lastly, in Hos 14:2-9, a call to conversion, and a promise from God of the forgiveness and abundant blessing of those who turn to the Lord. With this the book closes (Hos 14:1-9 :10). Thus we find again, that the contents of this last division fall very evidently into three parts (Hos 12:13, Hos 12:14, and Hos 14:2 -10), each of which is still further divisible into two strophes. <div eID="gen16260" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Israel’s Degeneracy into Canaanitish Ways - Hebrew_Bible_12:1-14 (English_Bible_ 11:12-12:14).</title> <div sID="gen16261" type="x-p"/> The faithlessness of Israel and Judah’s resistance to God bring righteous punishment upon the entire posterity of Jacob (11:12-12:2); whereas the example of their forefather ought to have led them to faithful attachment to their God (Hos 12:3-6). But Israel has become Canaan, and seeks its advantage in deception and injustice, without hearkening to its God or to the voice of its prophets, and will be punished for its idolatry (Hos 12:7-11). Whereas Jacob was obliged to flee, and to serve for a wife in Aram, Jehovah led Israel out of Egypt, and guarded it by prophets. Nevertheless this nation has excited His wrath, and will have to bear its guilt (vv.12-14). The two strophes of this chapter are 11:12-12:6 and 7-14. <div eID="gen16261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> (Hebrew_Bible_12:1). <hi type="italic">“Ephraim has surrounded me with lying, and the house of Israel with deceit: and Judah is moreover unbridled against God, and against the faithful Holy One.</hi> Hos 12:1 (Hebrew_Bible_v_2).<hi type="italic">Ephraim grazeth wind, and hunteth after the east: all the day it multiplies lying and desolation, and they make a covenant with Asshur, and oil is carried to Egypt.</hi> Hos 12:2. <hi type="italic">And Jehovah has a controversy with Judah, and to perform a visitation upon Jacob, according to his ways: according to his works will He repay him.” </hi> In the name of Jehovah, the prophet raises a charge against Israel once more. Lying and deceit are the terms which he applies, not so much to the idolatry which they preferred to the worship of Jehovah (ψευδῆ καὶ λατρείαν, Theod.), as to the hypocrisy with which Israel, in spite of its idolatry, claimed to be still the people of Jehovah, pretended to worship Jehovah under the image of a calf, and turned right into wrong.<note placement="foot">Calvin explains סבבני correctly thus: “that He (i.e., God) had experienced the manifold faithlessness of the Israelites in all kinds of ways.” He interprets the whole sentence as follows: “The Israelites had acted unfaithfully towards God, and resorted to deceits, and that not in one way only, or of only one kind; but just as a man might surround his enemy with a great army, so had they gathered together innumerable frauds, with which they attacked God on every side.”</note><hi type="italic">Bēth Yisrâ'ēl</hi> (the house of Israel) is the nation of the ten tribes, and is synonymous with Ephraim. The statement concerning Judah has been interpreted in different ways, because the meaning of רד is open to dispute. Luther’s rendering, “but Judah still holds fast to its God,” is based upon the rabbinical interpretation of רוּד, in the sense of רדה, to rule, which is decidedly false. According to the Arabic <hi type="italic">râd</hi>, the meaning of <hi type="italic">rūd</hi> is to ramble about (used of cattle that have broken loose, or have not yet been fastened up, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jer 2:31</reference>); <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, to cause to ramble about (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.40">Gen 27:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">Psa 55:3</reference>). Construed as it is here with עם, it means to ramble about in relation to God, i.e., to be unbridled or unruly towards God. עם, as in many other cases where reciprocal actions are referred to, standing towards or with a person: see Ewald, §217, <hi type="italic">h</hi>. קדושׁים נאמן, the faithful, holy God. <hi type="italic">Qedōshı̄m</hi> is used of God, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">Pro 9:10</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.24.19">Jos 24:19</reference>), as an intensive <hi type="italic">pluralis majestatis</hi>, construed with a singular adjective (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.19.4">Isa 19:4</reference>; 2Ki 19:4). נאמן, firm, faithful, trustworthy; the opposite of <hi type="italic">râd</hi>. Judah is unbridled towards the powerful God (<hi type="italic">'El</hi>), towards the Holy One, who, as the Faithful One, also proves Himself to be holy in relation to His people, both by the sanctification of those who embrace His salvation, and also by the judgment and destruction of those who obstinately resist the leadings of His grace. In <reference osisRef="Prov.9.1">Pro 9:1</reference> the lying and deceit of Israel are more fully described. רעה רוּח is not to entertain one’s self on wind, i.e., to take delight in vain things; but רעה means to eat or graze spiritually; and <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>, the wind, is equivalent to emptiness. The meaning therefore is, to strive eagerly after what is empty or vain; synonymous with <hi type="italic">râdaph</hi>, to pursue. קדים, the east wind, in Palestine a fierce tempestuous wind, which comes with burning heat from the desert of Arabia, and is very destructive to seeds and plants (compare <reference osisRef="Job.27.21">Job 27:21</reference>, and Wetzstein’s Appendix to Delitzsch’s <hi type="italic">Commentary on Job</hi>). It is used, therefore, as a figurative representation, not of vain hopes and ideals, that cannot possibly be reached, but of that destruction which Israel is bringing upon itself. “All the day,” i.e., continually, it multiplies lying and violence, through the sins enumerated in Hos 4:2, by which the kingdom is being internally broken up. Added to this, there is the seeking for alliances with the powers of the world, viz., Assyria and Egypt, by which it hopes to secure their help (Hos 5:13), but only brings about its own destruction. Oil is taken to Egypt from the land abounding in olives (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.8">Deu 8:8</reference>), not as tribute, but as a present, for the purpose of securing an ally in Egypt. This actually took place during the reign of Hoshea, who endeavoured to liberate himself from the oppression of Assyria by means of a treaty with Egypt (2Ki 17:4).<note placement="foot">Manger has given the meaning correctly thus: “He is looking back to the ambassadors sent by king Hoshea with splendid presents to the king of Egypt, to bring him over to his side, and induce him to send him assistance against the king of Assyria, although he had bound himself by a sacred treaty to submit to the sovereignty of the latter.” Compare also Hengstenberg’s <hi type="italic">Christology</hi>, vol. i. p. 164 transl., where he refutes the current opinion, that the words refer to two different parties in the nation, viz., an Assyrian and an Egyptian party, and correctly describes the circumstances thus: “The people being severely oppressed by Asshur, sometimes apply to Egypt for help against Asshur, and at other times endeavour to awaken friendly feelings in the latter.”</note> <div eID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16263" type="x-p"/> The Lord will repay both kingdoms for such conduct as this. But just as the attitude of Judah towards God is described more mildly than the guilt of Israel in Hos 11:12, so the punishment of the two is differently described in Hos 12:2. Jehovah has a trial with Judah, i.e., He has to reprove and punish its sins and transgressions (Hos 4:1). Upon Jacob, or Israel of the ten tribes (as in Hos 10:11), He has to perform a visitation, i.e., to punish it according to its ways and its deeds (cf. Hos 4:9). לפקד, it is to be visited, i.e., He must visit.
